title: #59 Stop Saying the Word Just
author: Barton, Craig
summary: Building on an earlier tip about eliminating the word "easy" from teacher language, Barton turns to "just" as an equally damaging verbal habit. He argues "just" carries the same implicit message as "easy": that the step being described requires no real thought, which can silence students who are actually struggling, since admitting difficulty with something framed as trivial feels like a bigger admission of failure. Simply resolving to say it less isn't enough, Barton suggests; he recommends telling students explicitly that the teacher is trying to cut the word and inviting them to catch any lapses, which both signals genuine care about how language affects them and sharpens students' own attention to the teacher's wording. He closes with a related target for elimination -- "I'm just a teacher" -- reframing it as another instance of the same self-minimising language habit, worth dropping for the profession's own sense of its complexity and value.
points: "Just" functions like "easy": it frames a step as requiring no thought, which discourages struggling students from admitting difficulty because it makes their confusion feel like a bigger failure.

Barton recommends making the elimination effort visible to students -- telling them the goal and inviting them to catch lapses -- rather than trying to self-correct silently, since this builds trust and models responsiveness to their experience.
The tip extends to teachers' self-talk, not just classroom language: "I'm just a teacher" is flagged as the same verbal tic applied to the profession itself.
The broader claim is that habitual minimising language shapes whether students feel safe disclosing confusion, not merely how a step is technically described.
quotes: Way back in Newsletter #2, I wrote about why we should try to remove the word “easy” from our teaching lexicon.
Just” suffers from the same problem as “easy”. It suggests the matter we are describing is trivial and can be done without any thought.
If they are finding it difficult, need a little more time, or don’t understand, are they really going to stop and tell us when we have described the step in such a way? I don’t think so.
Tell your students that you want to stop saying and why, and ask them to listen out for you falling off the wagon.
This not only shows them how much you care about your practice and its effect on them, but it might make them pay closer attention to the words you are saying.
More like you are just doing one of the most complex, demanding jobs imaginable, so be proud of that!
